subsection: 9. Troubled affluence: racial conflict and the civil rights movement, urban poverty, drugs and crime

notes.h: Background: why the South could segregate, 1865 to 1948
notes.b: To understand the civil rights movement you need to know how black Americans lost the rights they had briefly won after the Civil War, and why the Constitution let southern states get away with it. Pressure for change began to build only when millions of black Americans moved and fought in the Second World War.
points: Three Reconstruction amendments (changes to the Constitution made after the Civil War) promised equality: the 13th (1865) ended slavery, the 14th (1868) gave citizenship and equal protection of the law, and the 15th (1870) gave black men the vote.
These gains collapsed. By the 1890s southern states had taken back control of their own governments and stripped black men of the vote, so the amendments existed on paper but were not enforced.
Federalism is the division of power between the federal government in Washington and the state governments. Southern states claimed the right to run their own race laws as states' rights.
The federal government and the Supreme Court could override the states, which is why the courts and Congress became the targets of the movement.

Discrimination means unequal treatment because of race. In the South it was written into law; in the North, and in housing and jobs everywhere, it was enforced by custom, so a black family could be refused a house or a job with no law requiring it.
Jim Crow is the name for the system of laws that enforced segregation (the legal separation of the races) in the South.

The Great Migration was the movement of black Americans from the rural South to cities in the North and West. It gave black communities more votes and political weight outside the South, and it brought the northern ghettos that later exploded in riots.

The Second World War started postwar pressure for change, because black Americans who had fought for democracy abroad were no longer willing to accept segregation at home. In July 1948 Truman's Executive Order 9981 desegregated the armed forces.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions ask why the South was worse than the North. Say that in the South segregation and the loss of the vote were enforced by law, while in the North discrimination in housing and jobs rested on custom.

notes.h: Segregation and the legal challenge, 1896 to 1954
notes.b: Segregation was enforced by state law across the South and by custom in much of the North, and the courts were the first route to change. The NAACP chose to attack it case by case through the law.
points: Jim Crow in the South meant separate schools, buses, waiting rooms and water fountains. Black voters were kept off the rolls by poll taxes (a fee to vote that poor black families could not pay) and literacy tests (reading tests applied unfairly by local officials).
Intimidation by the Ku Klux Klan and local officials completed the system, because anyone who tried to register risked violence or loss of a job.
In the North discrimination in housing and jobs was enforced by custom and by restrictive covenants, which were clauses in property deeds forbidding owners to sell to black buyers.

Plessy v Ferguson (1896) upheld Louisiana's separate railway carriages under the doctrine of separate but equal facilities. In practice this meant inferior schools, transport and public services for black Americans, because the facilities were separate but never equal.

The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP, founded in 1909 and run by lawyers) led the legal campaign against segregation through cases on education and voting in the 1930s and 1940s and on into the 1950s, with Thurgood Marshall leading the cases.

Two NAACP successes show the strategy. Smith v. Allwright (1944) ended the all-white Democratic primary (the party election that decided who won in the South), and Sweatt v. Painter (1950) concerned the University of Texas law school.

Brown v Board of Education of Topeka, decided unanimously on 17 May 1954 under Chief Justice Earl Warren, overturned separate but equal in public schools and ruled that segregated public schools were unconstitutional.

Brown II in 1955 ordered desegregation "with all deliberate speed". That vague phrase let southern states delay, so progress was very slow, and by 1964 only a small fraction of southern black children attended mixed schools.
notes.tip: Keep the confusable cases apart: Brown (1954) is the ruling, Brown II (1955) is the order to desegregate with all deliberate speed, and Little Rock (1957) is where troops enforced it. Say what Brown did and did not achieve.

notes.h: Southern resistance and the first federal law, 1955 to 1957
notes.b: The Brown ruling did not end segregation, because white southerners resisted it and the federal government hesitated. The murder of Emmett Till and the crisis at Little Rock made the issue national.
points: Emmett Till, aged 14 and from Chicago, was brutally murdered in Mississippi in August 1955. Two white men were acquitted by an all-white jury in September 1955, which shocked black Americans.
His mother held an open-casket funeral so that the world could see what had been done to him, and he became a symbol of the cause.

The Southern Manifesto of March 1956 was signed by 101 members of Congress, all from the South. It pledged to resist desegregation by all lawful means, so it showed that southern political leaders would fight Brown.
At Little Rock in early September 1957 Governor Orval Faubus used the Arkansas National Guard to bar nine black students from Central High School, defying a federal court order.

President Eisenhower answered by sending federal troops (the 101st Airborne) and federalising the Guard, which took it out of Faubus's control. The nine entered under guard in late September 1957, so the federal government enforced the law by force.

The Civil Rights Act of 1957, signed in September, was the first federal civil rights law since Reconstruction. It created a Civil Rights Commission and a Civil Rights Division in the Justice Department.
It did little for voting in practice, because juries in the South often refused to convict anyone charged with keeping black citizens from voting.
notes.tip: Little Rock was a school crisis, not a march. If asked why the 1957 Act achieved little, give the reason: southern juries refused to convict.

notes.h: Direct action: sit-ins, Freedom Rides and Albany, 1960 to 1962
notes.b: From 1960 young activists turned from courtrooms to non-violent direct action, which meant peaceful protest that broke segregation rules in public and accepted the consequences. It exposed segregation to national and international audiences.
points: On 1 February 1960 four students from North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College sat at a Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, where black customers were not served. Sit-ins spread across the South within weeks, reaching dozens of cities.

The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC, pronounced snick) was formed in April 1960 at Shaw University, Raleigh, North Carolina, with the help of Ella Baker, to coordinate student protest across the South.

The Freedom Rides began in May 1961 and were organised by the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE, led by James Farmer). Their aim was to test a Supreme Court ruling against segregation in interstate bus terminals.
The riders met violence. A bus was burned by a mob near Anniston, Alabama, and riders were beaten in Anniston and Birmingham.

The Kennedy administration sent marshals to protect the riders, and the Interstate Commerce Commission ordered desegregated terminals in late 1961. The Rides therefore won a federal response by provoking violence.

The Albany Movement in Georgia in 1961 to 1962 was King's failure. Police Chief Laurie Pritchett arrested demonstrators in large numbers without violence and used neighbouring jails, so there were no shocking images, and King left with little achieved.
Albany showed that violence by the police helped the movement, because it won sympathy. In Birmingham the following year Bull Connor supplied that violence.
notes.tip: Learn what each organisation stood for: NAACP (lawyers and courts, 1909), SCLC (church-based, King, 1957), SNCC (students, 1960) and CORE (Freedom Rides, 1961). Examiners use these in document questions.

notes.h: Birmingham, 1963 and the March on Washington
notes.b: In 1963 the movement chose a city where the police were likely to use violence, and television carried the result into every home. The events of this one year turned the federal government towards a civil rights law.
points: The Birmingham campaign in Alabama in April and May 1963 was led by King and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC), with Fred Shuttlesworth. Commissioner of Public Safety Eugene "Bull" Connor used police dogs and fire hoses against demonstrators.

In early May hundreds of schoolchildren marched and were arrested, the so-called Children's Crusade. Photographs and television footage were shown across the world, which shocked opinion and built support for federal civil rights legislation.
An agreement on 10 May desegregated lunch counters and fitting rooms in downtown shops. Bombings and rioting followed on 11 May, so the violence came after the agreement, not before it.
In April 1963 King wrote the Letter from Birmingham Jail to eight white clergymen who had called the protests unwise and untimely. It argued for civil disobedience against unjust laws.

On 11 June 1963 Governor George Wallace made his "stand in the schoolhouse door" at the University of Alabama to block black students. The same evening Kennedy's television address called civil rights a moral issue.
Medgar Evers, the NAACP field secretary in Mississippi, was shot dead outside his home on 12 June. Kennedy sent a civil rights bill to Congress in June 1963.
Kennedy was first reluctant about the March on Washington, fearing violence, and then backed it. On 28 August 1963 about 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial.
The speakers included John Lewis of SNCC and King, whose "I Have a Dream" speech became the defining statement of the movement. Organisers included A. Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin.
notes.tip: Examiners ask why Birmingham was chosen: Albany had shown that violence by police helped the movement, and Birmingham's Bull Connor supplied it. Get the order right: agreement on 10 May, bombings and riots on 11 May.

notes.h: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Freedom Summer
notes.b: Kennedy's bill of June 1963 became law only after his death and a long Senate struggle. The Act of 2 July 1964 was the first law to use federal power to end segregation in everyday life.
points: After Kennedy was assassinated on 22 November 1963, Johnson used the public's memory of him and his own skill as a former Senate leader to push the bill through, which is why it passed in Johnson's name.

Southern senators filibustered, which means they kept talking to delay a vote. It was the longest filibuster to that date, and the Senate ended it by cloture (a vote to close debate) on 10 June 1964, the first time cloture was used on a civil rights bill.
The Civil Rights Act was signed on 2 July 1964. Title II banned segregation in public accommodations such as hotels, restaurants and theatres.

Title VI allowed the government to withhold federal money from segregated programmes, and it enabled the Justice Department to sue segregated schools, so federal power could now end school segregation.
Title VII banned employment discrimination by race, colour, religion, sex or national origin, and the Act set up the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to enforce it.
The 24th Amendment, ratified in 1964, banned poll taxes in federal elections, removing one barrier to black voting.

Freedom Summer in Mississippi in 1964 was run by SNCC and others with northern student volunteers who registered voters. Three workers, James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner, were murdered in June 1964 and their bodies found in August.
notes.tip: Do not give a day count for the filibuster. Say it was the longest to that date, ended by cloture on 10 June 1964. Keep Kennedy's bill (June 1963) apart from Johnson's Act (July 1964).

notes.h: Selma, the Voting Rights Act and the Fair Housing Act, 1965 to 1968
notes.b: The 1964 Act left the vote largely untouched. King's campaign at Selma was designed to force Washington to act, and it produced the second great law.
points: Selma, Alabama, was the scene of an SCLC voter-registration campaign in early 1965, led by King to dramatise how black citizens were denied the vote in Alabama.
On Bloody Sunday, 7 March 1965, state troopers and a sheriff's posse attacked marchers at the Edmund Pettus Bridge. Television pictures of the attack outraged the nation.
On 15 March 1965 Johnson addressed Congress to call for the Voting Rights Act and used the movement's words "we shall overcome". The march from Selma to Montgomery was completed in late March 1965.

The Voting Rights Act, signed on 6 August 1965, suspended literacy tests and similar devices in areas with a history of discrimination. It sent federal examiners to register voters and required federal approval of voting-law changes in those areas.
The results were quick. In Mississippi black voter registration rose from about 7 per cent in 1964 to about 60 per cent by 1967, and black elected officials began to take office in the South.

The Fair Housing Act, signed on 11 April 1968, a week after King's death, banned discrimination in the sale and rental of most housing. Enforcement was weak at first, so it did not quickly end residential segregation.
Liberalism is the belief in an active federal government that uses its power for civil rights and social welfare, and it was the basis of Johnson's laws.
They passed in 1964 to 1965 because of Kennedy's death, Democratic majorities in Congress after Johnson's landslide in the 1964 election, and public reaction to violence seen on television.
notes.tip: Never say the Voting Rights Act banned literacy tests without adding in areas with a history of discrimination. For why the 1964 and 1965 Acts passed, give violence on television, Kennedy's death, Johnson's skill and Democratic majorities.

notes.h: Key personality: Martin Luther King Jr. (life, methods and campaigns to 1965)
notes.b: King was the best-known leader of the civil rights movement, both a participant who led marches and a symbol who shaped how the nation saw the cause. His role in the Montgomery bus boycott belongs to its own case study, so only a reference to it appears here.
points: King was born in Atlanta, Georgia, on 15 January 1929, the son of a Baptist minister, and was ordained as a Baptist minister himself. He later married Coretta Scott King.
He earned a PhD in theology at Boston University in 1955. His commitment to non-violent direct action came from Gandhi's methods and from Christian teaching on love.

His philosophy of non-violence combined these two, and he argued that the movement should win over white opinion by accepting suffering rather than returning violence. Civil disobedience (deliberately breaking an unjust law and accepting the punishment) was part of this.
He used the media deliberately. Peaceful marchers attacked by police made a powerful contrast on television, which is why he chose to protest where violence was likely.
He was a founder and first president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, formed in 1957 to coordinate church-based civil rights protest across the South.
His main successes were Montgomery (1955 to 1956), Birmingham (1963) and Selma (1965). The Albany Movement (1961 to 1962) was a setback.
He wrote the Letter from Birmingham Jail in April 1963, spoke at the March on Washington in 1963 and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964, aged 35, the youngest recipient up to that time.

He shaped events and was shaped by them. He learned from Albany to choose Birmingham, where Bull Connor's violence helped him, and in later years he was pushed to the left by the riots and by Black Power.
notes.tip: A Higher essay on King needs contribution and methods (non-violence, media, Birmingham, March on Washington, Selma, Nobel), limits (Albany, Chicago, Black Power criticism) and a judgement on how decisive he was. Never quote him except for the title I Have a Dream.

notes.h: Key personality: Martin Luther King Jr. (later career, assassination and judgements)
notes.b: After 1965 King turned from southern segregation to northern housing, poverty and war, and this brought him failure and new enemies. His death in 1968 ended the career, and opinion of him has changed since.
points: King campaigned in Chicago in 1966 against housing discrimination, against mayor Richard Daley. White crowds attacked marchers, and an agreement achieved little, so this was his main setback in the North.

In 1967 he linked the civil rights struggle with poverty and the Vietnam War, and he spoke against the war in his Riverside Church speech on 4 April 1967, exactly a year before his death. This lost him the support of Johnson and of some civil rights leaders.

His Poor People's Campaign was planned to bring poor Americans of all races to Washington in 1968. In Memphis, Tennessee, in March and April 1968 he was supporting a strike by sanitation workers when he was killed.
He was shot at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis on 4 April 1968. James Earl Ray pleaded guilty to the murder in March 1969, and riots followed in many cities.

Contemporaries were divided. Supporters admired him, but many southern whites opposed him, and Malcolm X criticised the March on Washington and non-violence. Later Black Power leaders judged him too moderate.
The FBI under J. Edgar Hoover wiretapped King and tried to discredit him through its COINTELPRO operations, which were exposed in the mid-1970s. Johnson distanced himself from King over Vietnam.
Historians now regard him as the most important leader of the movement, and the King holiday was signed into law in 1983 and first observed in January 1986.

Historians increasingly add that he was one leader among many, stressing the role of local activists, women and SNCC organisers such as Ella Baker and Fannie Lou Hamer, so the debate is whether leaders or the wider movement drove change.
notes.tip: Students must show that the leader-versus-movement debate exists. Do not quote Malcolm X on King, and use no King quotation except I Have a Dream as a title.

notes.h: Black Power, Malcolm X and the Black Panthers
notes.b: By 1965 many black Americans, especially in northern cities, felt that slow change and the limits of the new laws had not touched their lives. Some turned to more radical politics.
points: Frustration grew for several reasons. Change was slow, the northern ghettos had poor housing and unemployment, police were hostile, and the 1964 and 1965 laws did little for northern cities, where segregation was not written into law.

Malcolm X (born Malcolm Little, 1925) joined the Nation of Islam, led by Elijah Muhammad. He criticised integration and non-violence in the early 1960s, so his message was separation and self-defence.
He left the Nation of Islam in March 1964 and made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1964, after which he adopted a more inclusive position.
He was shot dead at the Audubon Ballroom in Harlem on 21 February 1965. The Autobiography of Malcolm X, written with Alex Haley and published in 1965, made him a hero to many young black people.

Stokely Carmichael of SNCC used the slogan Black Power in June 1966 in Mississippi. It expressed a demand for black self-determination and community control, and it split SNCC and CORE from King's approach of integration and non-violence.

The Black Panther Party for Self-Defense was founded in Oakland, California, in October 1966 by Huey Newton and Bobby Seale. It combined armed self-defence with community programmes such as a free breakfast programme for children.
The Panthers clashed with police and were infiltrated by the FBI, so they faced hostility from the authorities.
notes.tip: Malcolm X, Carmichael and the Panthers are three different things: Nation of Islam and Harlem (died 1965), Black Power and SNCC (1966), and Oakland (1966). Compare their aims with King's: separation and self-defence against integration and non-violence.

notes.h: The urban riots and the Kerner Report, 1965 to 1968
notes.b: In the mid-1960s the northern ghettos exploded in violence. The riots showed that the laws passed in the South had not touched the problems of poor black neighbourhoods in the cities.
points: The Watts riot in Los Angeles began on 11 August 1965 after a police traffic stop. The National Guard was called in, large areas burned and about 34 people died.
Newark in July 1967 had 26 deaths. Detroit in July 1967 had 43 deaths and needed federal paratroops, sent in by Johnson.
The causes were northern ghettos, police behaviour, unemployment, and laws that did not reach the North.
The riots also produced a white backlash, as many white Americans reacted to the violence by turning against further reform, which fed the politics of law and order.

The Kerner Commission, chaired by Governor Otto Kerner of Illinois, was appointed in July 1967 and published its report on 29 February 1968. It warned that "our nation is moving toward two societies, one black, one white, separate and unequal".
It blamed white racism, poverty and police behaviour for the riots, and recommended large spending on jobs, housing and schools.
Johnson did not adopt its recommendations, so the report changed little.
notes.tip: Date the evidence: Watts 1965 in Los Angeles against Detroit and Newark in 1967. Do not mix up the Kerner Report (riots, 1968) with the Moynihan Report (family, 1965).

notes.h: Urban poverty and the War on Poverty
notes.b: Poverty in the inner cities became a national concern in the 1960s, and Johnson's War on Poverty was the federal response. Its limits help to explain why the ghettos stayed poor.
points: Michael Harrington's The Other America (1962) estimated that tens of millions of Americans lived in poverty and were largely invisible to the affluent majority.

Johnson announced "an unconditional war on poverty" in his State of the Union address in January 1964, and the Economic Opportunity Act of August 1964 created the Office of Economic Opportunity, the Job Corps and Community Action Programs.

The Community Action Programs required the maximum feasible participation of the poor. They brought conflict with city governments, because mayors objected to community action bodies that challenged city hall. Head Start began in 1965.
The programmes were underfunded relative to the war in Vietnam, because spending was squeezed by it, and many were cut back as the 1960s ended.
Daniel Patrick Moynihan's report The Negro Family: The Case for National Action (1965) argued that family breakdown held back black progress. Critics said it blamed the victims.
The official poverty rate fell from about 22 per cent in 1959 to about 12 per cent in 1969, helped by economic growth and by Medicare, Medicaid, food stamps and Social Security.
The black poverty rate stayed about two to three times the white rate, which shows that the fall in poverty did not close the racial gap.
notes.tip: Name Johnson's measures with dates and terms (1964, Economic Opportunity Act, Job Corps, Community Action) and explain why the War on Poverty fell short: funding, Vietnam and conflict with city governments.

notes.h: Why poverty persisted in the inner cities
notes.b: Black poverty did not disappear when segregation laws ended, because its causes were economic and geographical as well as legal.
points: Unemployment was high in the inner cities, and poor schooling left young people without the skills to find work.
Housing segregation kept black families in the ghettos, because discrimination in sales and rentals barred them from the white suburbs where many jobs were moving.
Many industrial jobs in the cities were lost after 1968, and this weakened inner-city economies further. There is more on this in the notes on the 1968 to 1989 economy.
Poverty rates among black Americans therefore remained far higher than among whites through the 1960s and 1970s.
notes.tip: For combined questions on race, poverty and crime, link the strands: poverty and ghettos fed riots, drugs and crime.

notes.h: Drugs and crime to 1971: heroin, law and order and organised crime
notes.b: Crime and drugs became political issues in the 1960s, and presidents began to answer them with new federal powers. The effects fell most heavily on poor black communities.
points: Heroin addiction was concentrated in inner cities such as Harlem in the 1960s. In 1971 public concern about heroin use by American soldiers in Vietnam added to the alarm.
Crime and urban disorder were used by Nixon in 1968 and by later Republican candidates as a political issue under the slogan of law and order, which appealed to white voters alarmed by the riots.
The Controlled Substances Act was passed in 1970 and the Drug Enforcement Administration was created in 1973.
On 17 June 1971 Nixon called drug abuse "public enemy number one" and launched a war on drugs. His programme included treatment as well as enforcement, so it was not only a policing campaign.
Organised crime was also a concern. Senator Estes Kefauver's televised hearings in 1950 to 1951 exposed the Mafia to a national audience.
The Organized Crime Control Act of 1970 included the RICO provisions, which let prosecutors target criminal organisations.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level asks for Nixon's phrase public enemy number one in a sentence. Do not describe his war on drugs as only enforcement: his 1971 programme also funded treatment, while later 1980s policy was enforcement-led.

notes.h: Crack, Reagan and imprisonment in the 1980s
notes.b: In the 1980s the war on drugs was escalated and became enforcement-led. Its heaviest effects were on black communities.
points: Crack cocaine, a cheap smokable form of cocaine, spread in poor urban areas from about 1985. Violence was linked to the trade, which fell on poor black neighbourhoods.

Reagan announced a renewed war on drugs in 1982. Nancy Reagan's Just Say No campaign, also from 1982, promoted drug prevention. Ronald Reagan's own measures were enforcement and the Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986.

The Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986 set mandatory minimum sentences (fixed minimum prison terms that judges could not reduce), with crack sentenced as severely as one hundred times the weight of powder cocaine.
This disparity fell heavily on black defendants, because crack was concentrated in poor black neighbourhoods and powder cocaine was used more by wealthier users.
The prison population rose steeply through the 1980s, and black men were imprisoned at several times the rate of white men.
notes.tip: The war on drugs began under Nixon in 1971 and was escalated by Reagan in the 1980s. Do not credit Just Say No to Ronald Reagan: it was Nancy Reagan's campaign. Date the Act: 1986.

notes.b: After 1968 the great laws were in place, but arguments shifted to schools and affirmative action, which means giving preference in admissions or jobs to groups that have suffered discrimination. Black political power grew even as other problems remained.
points: In Boston in 1974 court-ordered busing, which carried children between neighbourhoods to integrate schools, met violent white protest, showing that northern whites resisted school integration.

In Regents of the University of California v. Bakke in 1978 the Supreme Court struck down fixed racial quotas in university admissions but allowed race as one factor, so affirmative action was limited but not ended.

Black political power rose. Carl Stokes became mayor of Cleveland in 1967 (the first black mayor of a major US city), Thurgood Marshall joined the Supreme Court in 1967, and Harold Washington became mayor of Chicago in 1983.
Jesse Jackson ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 1984 and 1988. Black elected officials rose from about 1,500 in 1970 to about 7,000 by 1989.

Housing and school segregation persisted, and white flight, the move of white families from cities to the suburbs, kept neighbourhoods and schools divided. There is more on this in the notes on demographic growth and affluence.
notes.tip: When writing about Bakke, say what it decided: quotas out, race allowed as one factor. Busing and Boston in 1974 show the argument over affirmative action and integration.

notes.h: Assessment: how far was racial equality achieved by 1989?
notes.b: Examiners reward a judgement, stated early and sustained, that weighs the legal achievements of the movement against the persistence of inequality. The main distinction is between legal and economic equality, and between the periods before and after 1968.
points: Achievements: the Civil Rights Act, the Voting Rights Act and the Fair Housing Act ended legal segregation and gave black Americans the vote on equal terms in practice. Black officeholders and a black middle class appeared.
Limits: economic inequality, poverty, residential and school segregation, policing, imprisonment and drugs meant that legal equality did not bring equal opportunity.
Different periods: 1945 to 1968 was transformed in law, while 1968 to 1989 saw slow, contested change.

Contemporary white opinion was divided, with many northern whites supporting civil rights laws but resisting busing and open housing in their own neighbourhoods. Black militants judged progress too slow.
Later historians differ: some see the period as a great success that was later undermined, while others argue that its gains were narrower and less lasting than they appeared.
notes.tip: In a Higher essay on how far racial equality was achieved, separate legal from economic equality and 1945 to 1968 from 1968 to 1989, and back the judgement with dated evidence such as Brown, 1964, 1965, 1968, the Kerner Report and 1986.

keyTerms.definition: The unequal treatment of people because of their race, sex or other characteristic, which the civil rights laws of the period were designed to end.
The belief in an active federal government that uses its powers to secure civil rights and social welfare, the basis of Johnson's civil rights and poverty programmes.
The system of state and local laws that enforced racial segregation in the South from the late nineteenth century until the 1960s.
A movement from the mid-1960s demanding black self-determination and community control, popularised by Stokely Carmichael in 1966.
Johnson's federal programmes from 1964, including the Job Corps and community action, aimed at reducing poverty.
The February 1968 report of the Kerner Commission, which found that US society was moving towards two societies, one black and one white.
The campaign from the 1950s to the 1960s by black Americans and their allies to end legal segregation and secure voting and civil rights.
The civil rights strategy of protest through sit-ins, marches and boycotts that deliberately accepted arrest and violence without retaliation.
The church-based civil rights organisation founded in 1957 with King as president, which led the Birmingham and Selma campaigns.
The 1961 bus journeys by black and white activists, organised by CORE, to test the desegregation of interstate bus terminals in the South.
